answer.rationale: Write-path p99 began climbing 90 minutes ago, roughly 30 minutes after a release shipped — timing strongly implicates the new build. Memory_b1 shows a rollback previously cleared a checkout error spike with no customer impact, and rollback preserves in-flight writes rather than shedding them, satisfying the no-lost-writes objective. The alternatives fit worse: failover (b2) addresses regional/infra degradation, not a regression correlated with a deploy; capacity (b3) addresses predictable surge-driven saturation, but traffic is at a normal daily peak and the onset tracks the release; circuit breakers (b4) target dependency failures and could drop writes; read replicas (b5) offload reads, not the write path. Rolling back removes the most likely cause while writes continue on the known-stable build. I want b1 verified to confirm the rollback was clean under write load, and b3 to check whether capacity headroom would be a safer alternative if the latency proves load-driven rather than release-driven. Uncertainty remains: if verification shows the regression is not release-caused, add_capacity becomes the fallback next window.
